categories.name: Ownership & Borrowing
categories.description: Move semantics, lifetimes, borrowing rules, and smart pointers in idiomatic Rust.

cards.question: What problem does Rust ownership solve?
cards.answer: Each value has a single owner; when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped exactly once. This eliminates double-free and use-after-free without a garbage collector. Borrowing lets temporary shared or exclusive access without transferring ownership. The borrow checker enforces these rules at compile time.

cards.question: What is the difference between move and copy in Rust?
cards.answer: Types implementing Copy duplicate bits on assignment; most primitives and small aggregates are Copy. Non-Copy types move ownership, leaving the source unusable unless it implements Default or was partially moved. Clone is explicit deep duplication when needed. Accidental moves of large buffers show up as use-after-move compile errors.

cards.question: When do you need lifetime annotations on function signatures?
cards.answer: When the compiler cannot infer how long references in parameters and return values relate. Common with functions returning slices or references into inputs. Elision rules cover many simple cases like fn foo(x: &str) -> &str with one input lifetime. Incorrect annotations fail to compile rather than dangling at runtime.

cards.question: Compare Box, Rc, and Arc for sharing data.
cards.answer: Box owns heap data uniquely with known size on the stack. Rc shares ownership on single-threaded code with reference counting. Arc is thread-safe Rc using atomic refcounts for multi-threaded sharing. Choose Arc<Mutex<T>> or channels when threads mutate shared state.

cards.question: What is interior mutability and Cell versus RefCell?
cards.answer: Interior mutability allows mutation through shared references when runtime checks or Copy rules guarantee safety. Cell wraps Copy types with get/set without references. RefCell provides runtime borrow flags for non-Copy data and panics on double mutable borrow. Mutex extends the idea across threads with blocking.

cards.question: Explain the 'static' lifetime and when it appears.
cards.answer: 'static means the reference lives for the entire program, like string literals stored in the binary. Owned String can be leaked to 'static with Box::leak for global config but rarely should. Trait bounds T: 'static often mean no borrowed data in async tasks. Confusing 'static with const or global variables is a common mistake.

cards.question: What is borrowing mutably versus immutably?
cards.answer: Any number of immutable borrows OR exactly one mutable borrow may exist at a time for a given value. Mutable borrows exclude readers, enabling exclusive updates without data races. Splitting borrows across struct fields uses disjoint field borrowing automatically in many patterns. Iterator methods often take &mut self exploiting this rule.

cards.question: How does Drop interact with panic and unwinding?
cards.answer: Drop runs when values leave scope, including during stack unwinding from panic unless abort strategy is set. Drop order is reverse declaration order for struct fields. Implement Drop for RAII around files and locks; avoid panicking inside Drop. Manually mem::forget skips Drop when you must leak intentionally.

cards.question: What is Cow and when is it useful?
cards.answer: Clone-on-write enum either borrows immutably or owns a cloned buffer when mutation is needed. Ideal for APIs accepting &str or String-like inputs without forcing allocation upfront. Parsing pipelines use Cow to stay borrow-only on happy paths. Conversion to owned happens lazily on first write.

cards.question: Why can returning references to local variables fail to compile?
cards.answer: Local variables die at function end, so any reference to them would dangle. Rust rejects these unless lifetimes tie returns to inputs. Returning owned values or 'static references fixes the issue. This compile-time check replaces many C++ return-reference footguns.

cards.question: What is ownership rules?
cards.answer: Rust ownership ensures each value has one owner and references obey borrow rules at compile time. Moves transfer ownership; borrows grant temporary access with aliasing limits. Lifetime annotations tie references to valid data and prevent use-after-free.

cards.question: How do Result and Option differ from exceptions?
cards.answer: Errors are values carried in Result<T, E> that callers must handle explicitly. Option models absence without null pointers. This makes control flow visible and documents failure modes in types. ? propagates errors ergonomically while staying explicit in signatures.

cards.question: What is the difference between impl Trait and dyn Trait?
cards.answer: impl Trait in return position hides a concrete type statically resolved at compile time with monomorphization. dyn Trait is a fat pointer with vtable for runtime polymorphism on the heap or stack via references. impl Trait is zero-cost; dyn Trait adds indirection but enables heterogeneous collections. async fn returns opaque impl Future types similarly.

cards.question: When do you derive traits versus implement manually?
cards.answer: Derive works for Debug, Clone, PartialEq, and many standard traits when fields support them. Manual impls customize behavior like ordering not matching equality or Send bounds. Newtype wrappers derive on inner fields with transparent semantics. Orphan rules require local newtypes to implement foreign traits.

cards.question: Explain the orphan rule for trait implementations.
cards.answer: You may implement a trait for a type only if you own the trait or the type in your crate. Prevents conflicting impls across crates for the same pair. Wrapper types around foreign types are the idiomatic extension point. Blanket impls like impl<T: Display> ToString are powerful but can break coherence if overlapping.

cards.question: What are associated types in traits?
cards.answer: They name output types inside a trait, like Iterator::Item. One impl per type determines associated types unlike generic methods with multiple type params. They simplify signatures for iterators and async streams. GATs generalize associated types to lifetimes and generics on traits.

cards.question: How does pattern matching with enums improve safety?
cards.answer: match must cover all variants, so refactors adding variants become compile errors until handled. Option and Result force nil handling at call sites. Destructuring nested enums clarifies protocol state machines. if let and while let sugar common single-pattern cases.

cards.question: What is From and Into used for?
cards.answer: From enables one-way conversions with impl From<A> for B and auto Into. Prefer From for clear conversion direction in APIs accepting impl Into<T>. TryFrom handles fallible conversions without panics. They reduce boilerplate compared to ad hoc constructor functions.

cards.question: How do you model errors in a library crate?
cards.answer: Define a small enum or struct error type implementing std::error::Error and Display. thiserror reduces boilerplate; anyhow suits applications aggregating errors. Libraries avoid anyhow in public APIs to keep errors typed for callers. Provide context with map_err and #[source] chains.

cards.question: What is zero-sized type (ZST) usage?
cards.answer: Types like () or marker structs consume no runtime space but carry type information. PhantomData marks ownership of lifetimes or types without storing them. State machine types encode protocol phases in the type system. Misusing ZST markers can still affect codegen via monomorphization.

cards.question: When prefer enum over trait object for variants?
cards.answer: Closed sets of variants with known behavior fit enums with match exhaustiveness. Open extension across crates favors traits and dyn. Enums enable inlined dispatch without vtable indirection. Hybrid approaches use enum of boxed dyn for plugin registries.

cards.question: How do you apply Result in day-to-day Types & Traits work?
cards.answer: Result<T, E> models success or failure as values, forcing callers to handle errors explicitly. The ? operator propagates errors ergonomically while keeping signatures honest. Libraries expose typed errors; applications may aggregate with anyhow-style wrappers at the boundary.

categories.name: Async & Concurrency
categories.description: async/await, executors, channels, and safe parallelism patterns.

cards.question: What does async fn desugar to in Rust?
cards.answer: An async fn returns impl Future<Output = T> that runs incrementally when polled. The compiler transforms await points into state machine code. Nothing executes until the future is spawned on a runtime or awaited. async blocks capture variables similarly to closures.

cards.question: What is Send and Sync and why do they matter for async?
cards.answer: Send types can move across thread boundaries; Sync means shared references are Send. Async tasks often require Send because executors may migrate them between threads. Rc and RefCell are not Send; Arc and Mutex are. Non-Sync futures cannot be held across await in multi-thread runtimes without care.

cards.question: Compare tokio::spawn versus block_on for CLI tools.
cards.answer: block_on runs a runtime on the current thread until the future completes, suitable for small binaries. spawn schedules concurrent tasks on worker threads for servers. Mixing block_on inside async tasks can deadlock nested runtimes. Prefer tokio::main or async main for consistent entry.

cards.question: How do mpsc channels differ from async channels in tokio?
cards.answer: std::sync::mpsc blocks threads; async channels await send and recv without blocking threads. Bounded channels apply backpressure when consumers lag producers. select! merges multiple async sources for timeouts and cancellation. Choose channel depth from memory and latency budgets.

cards.question: What causes async cancellation and how handle it?
cards.answer: Dropping a future stops polling at next await, potentially leaving resources open. Use scopes like tokio::select! with explicit shutdown or Drop guards for locks. tokio::time::timeout wraps slow operations. Structured concurrency crates group child tasks lifetimes with parents.

cards.question: When use Mutex versus RwLock in async code?
cards.answer: Async Mutex from tokio yields the task instead of blocking threads when contended. Std Mutex in async can stall the executor if held across await points. RwLock helps read-heavy caches with occasional writes. Keep critical sections short and never await while holding std locks.

cards.question: What is pin and why are some futures Unpin-sensitive?
cards.answer: Self-referential async state machines must not move after poll starts; Pin fixes address in memory. Most futures are Unpin and need no special handling. Pin<Box<dyn Future>> is common for heap-stored trait objects. Violating pin contracts causes subtle use-after-move bugs.

cards.question: How does rayon parallelize CPU-bound work from async servers?
cards.answer: rayon thread pools run compute jobs without blocking async worker threads. spawn_blocking in tokio offloads blocking IO and heavy CPU similarly. Keep async tasks for IO multiplexing; delegate matmul or compression to dedicated pools. Oversubscription hurts when both stacks fight for cores.

cards.question: Explain atomics and Ordering for lock-free counters.
cards.answer: AtomicU64 fetch_add with Ordering::Relaxed is enough for statistics. Release-acquire pairs publish data visible to other threads after counters increment. SeqCst is simplest but slower; use when reasoning cost is high. Lock-free structures still require careful design beyond atomics alone.

cards.question: What is a common pitfall with std::thread::sleep in async services?
cards.answer: sleep blocks an OS thread, reducing executor capacity under load. Use tokio::time::sleep for async delays that yield the task. Long blocking calls belong in spawn_blocking with limits. Timeouts should integrate with cancellation tokens for graceful shutdown.

categories.name: Unsafe & FFI
categories.description: FFI, unsafe Rust, memory layout, and building reliable low-level components.

cards.question: When is unsafe required in Rust?
cards.answer: For dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions, accessing mutable statics, and implementing unsafe traits. Safe abstractions can wrap unsafe internals if invariants are enforced at API boundaries. unsafe does not disable the borrow checker; it trusts the programmer for listed operations. Minimize unsafe blocks and document safety preconditions.

cards.question: How do you call C libraries from Rust safely?
cards.answer: Use bindgen or manual extern blocks for signatures and link native libs. Wrap raw pointers in structs with Drop for resource cleanup. Validate C API preconditions before unsafe calls and convert errors to Result. Test FFI on all target platforms in CI.

cards.question: What is MaybeUninit and why avoid uninitialized reads?
cards.answer: MaybeUninit<T> reserves memory without claiming T is initialized, avoiding undefined behavior on large structs. assume_init reads after you prove initialization. Useful for buffers filled by IO or C callbacks. mem::zeroed is only safe for types allowing all-zero bit patterns.

cards.question: Explain repr(C) and layout compatibility.
